caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: São Tomé and Príncipe's debt was among the world's highest before relief: 283.2% of GDP in 2006, the series high. HIPC/MDRI completion in 2007 brought it down to 61.0% by 2008, and it has fluctuated in the 55-105% range since, reaching a projected 55.7% in 2025, the post-relief low. The government borrows concessionally and from Portugal and Taiwan; oil exploration hopes in the Joint Development Zone with Nigeria never materialized into revenues. At 56% of GDP for a microstate with almost no exports, the debt is a permanent constraint, and IMF assessments flag high risk of distress; the economy survives on aid, cocoa, and tourism.
inflation_management: São Tomé and Príncipe's inflation was tamed by the dobra's peg to the euro (since 2010). It ran at 18-32% in 2006-2008, the series high of 32.0% in 2008, on food and fuel prices and monetary instability. The peg brought it down steadily to 5-8% through the 2010s, and the 2022 global shock pushed it back to 18.1% in 2022 and 21.1% in 2023 before collapsing to a projected 0.9% in 2025, the series low. The euro peg is the anchor of the entire macro framework; without it, a microstate with no exports would have no nominal anchor at all.

key_events.event: HIPC completion-point relief cut debt from 283.2% to about 61% of GDP.
Dobra pegged to the euro, ending the high-inflation era.
Oil exploration in the Nigeria joint zone yielded no commercial finds; hopes faded.
COVID-19 devastated tourism; debt climbed back above 90% of GDP.
Failed coup attempt (November 2022); political instability persisted.
Inflation projected at 0.9%, the series low, as the peg and weak demand contained prices.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued aid-dependent stagnation with low inflation under the euro peg and debt near 55% of GDP. Upside is limited to tourism and any offshore oil surprise; downside is donor fatigue or another shock to a state with no buffers. Uncertainty is moderate: the peg is credible and politics are democratic, but the economy is too small to generate its own momentum.
